claim: Stromules are tubular extensions from chloroplasts that have been observed in several genera in the plant kingdom.
source: Stroma-filled tubular structures called stromules emanate from chloroplasts and have been observed in several genera in the plant kingdom, although they are most common in non-green plastids (Gray et al., 2001; Hanson and Sattarzadeh, 2008; Köhler and Hanson, 2000; Kumar et al., 2014; Natesan et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Stromules are most common in non-green plastids.
source: Stroma-filled tubular structures called stromules emanate from chloroplasts and have been observed in several genera in the plant kingdom, although they are most common in non-green plastids (Gray et al., 2001; Hanson and Sattarzadeh, 2008; Köhler and Hanson, 2000; Kumar et al., 2014; Natesan et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Stromules are developmentally regulated and induced in response to biotic and abiotic stress, symbiotic association, and changes in plastid number and size.
source: Stromules are developmentally regulated and induced in response to biotic and abiotic stress, symbiotic association, and changes in plastid number and size (Brunkard et al., 2015; Caplan et al., 2015; Caplan et al., 2008; Erickson et al., 2014; Gray et al., 2012; Kumar et al., 2014; Schattat and Klösgen, 2011; Waters et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: The dynamic extension of stromules increases the surface area of chloroplasts.
source: The dynamic extension of stromules increases the surface area of chloroplasts, presumably facilitating transport of signals or macromolecules to the nucleus, cytosol, plasma membrane or other organelles (Gunning, 2005, 2004a; Kwok and Hanson, 2004c).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature and represents a logical inference about the functional consequence of increased surface area.

claim: Stromules are induced and function during innate immunity.
source: We have recently shown that stromules are induced and function during innate immunity (Caplan et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Induced stromules make connections with nuclei to facilitate transport of chloroplast-localized defense protein NRIP1 and hydrogen peroxide from chloroplasts into nuclei during an immune response.
source: The induced stromules make connections with the nuclei to facilitate transport of chloroplast-localized defense protein NRIP1 (N receptor interacting protein 1) and the pro-defense molecule, hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), from chloroplasts into nuclei during an immune response (Caplan et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Stromules may facilitate certain number of chloroplasts to maintain contact with moving nuclei.
source: Stromules may also facilitate certain number of chloroplasts to maintain contact with the moving nuclei (Erickson et al., 2017a).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature and is presented as speculative ('may').

claim: The mechanism(s) that facilitates chloroplast stromules connections to nuclei and eventual perinuclear clustering of chloroplasts is unknown.
source: However, the mechanism(s) that facilitates chloroplast stromules connections to nuclei and eventual perinuclear clustering of chloroplasts is unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Stromule length is variable as they extend, retract and branch, changing their shape and position.
source: Stromule length is variable as they extend, retract and branch, changing their shape and position (Gray et al., 2001; Gunning, 2005; Kwok and Hanson, 2004c; Waters et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Mechanisms that regulate the dynamic nature of stromule morphology and motility are poorly understood.
source: However, mechanisms that regulate the dynamic nature of stromule morphology and motility are poorly understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Studies using inhibitors in non-green tissue have implicated cytoskeleton elements such as actin microfilaments (AFs) and microtubules (MTs) in regulating stromule frequency, length and motility.
source: Studies using inhibitors in non-green tissue have implicated cytoskeleton elements such as actin microfilaments (AFs) and microtubules (MTs) in regulating stromule frequency, length and motility (Gunning, 2005; Kwok and Hanson, 2003; Kwok and Hanson, 2004a).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Treatment with AF inhibitors, Cytochalasin D (CTD) and Latrunculin B, resulted in the reduction of stromule frequency in tobacco hypocotyls.
source: Treatment with AF inhibitors, Cytochalasin D (CTD) and Latrunculin B, resulted in the reduction of stromule frequency in tobacco hypocotyls (Kwok and Hanson, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Stromules have been observed to extend parallel to AFs in Arabidopsis hypocotyl epidermal cells.
source: Stromules have been observed to extend parallel to AFs and the tips of stromules make contact with AFs in Arabidopsis hypocotyl epidermal cells (Kwok and Hanson, 2004a).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The tips of stromules make contact with AFs in Arabidopsis hypocotyl epidermal cells.
source: Stromules have been observed to extend parallel to AFs and the tips of stromules make contact with AFs in Arabidopsis hypocotyl epidermal cells (Kwok and Hanson, 2004a).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Treatment with myosin ATPase inhibitor 2,3 butanedione 2-monoxime (BDM) affects stromule movement and length.
source: Treatment with myosin ATPase inhibitor 2,3 butanedione 2-monoxime (BDM) affects stromule movement and length; furthermore, Myosin XI family motor proteins have been implicated in stromule movement and anchoring to the cytoskeleton in Nicotiana (Natesan et al., 2009; Sattarzadeh et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Myosin XI family motor proteins have been implicated in stromule movement and anchoring to the cytoskeleton in Nicotiana.
source: Treatment with myosin ATPase inhibitor 2,3 butanedione 2-monoxime (BDM) affects stromule movement and length; furthermore, Myosin XI family motor proteins have been implicated in stromule movement and anchoring to the cytoskeleton in Nicotiana (Natesan et al., 2009; Sattarzadeh et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Direct evidence for stromule movement along AFs is lacking.
source: These findings suggest that stromules move along AFs using myosin motors; however, direct evidence for movement along AFs is lacking.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Treatment with MT inhibitor amiprophosmethyl (APM) reduced stromules.
source: Treatment with MT inhibitor amiprophosmethyl (APM) reduced stromules, and co-treatment with AF and MT inhibitors decreased stromule frequency and length (Kwok and Hanson, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Co-treatment with AF and MT inhibitors decreased stromule frequency and length.
source: Treatment with MT inhibitor amiprophosmethyl (APM) reduced stromules, and co-treatment with AF and MT inhibitors decreased stromule frequency and length (Kwok and Hanson, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Chloroplast protrusions from mesophyll chloroplasts of the arctic plant Oxyria digyna remained unaffected by the MT inhibitor Oryzalin or the AF inhibitor LatB.
source: In contrast, 'chloroplast protrusions' from mesophyll chloroplasts of the arctic plant Oxyria digyna remained unaffected by the MT inhibitor Oryzalin or the AF inhibitor LatB (Holzinger et al., 2007b).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The precise role of AFs and MTs during stromule dynamics in green tissue chloroplasts is not well understood.
source: Therefore, the precise role of AFs and MTs during stromule dynamics in green tissue chloroplasts is not well understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: MTs are required for stromule extension and movement.
source: Our results show that MTs are required for stromule extension and movement.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including inhibitor studies and time-lapse imaging.

claim: MT depolymerization led to stromule retraction.
source: MT depolymerization led to stromule retraction, and MT stabilization increased stromule frequency.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript using MT depolymerizing agents.

claim: MT stabilization increased stromule frequency.
source: MT depolymerization led to stromule retraction, and MT stabilization increased stromule frequency.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript using Paclitaxel.

claim: Silencing the gene for γ-tubulin complex protein 4 (GCP4) caused enhanced bundling and disrupted dynamics of MTs.
source: Silencing the gene for γ-tubulin complex protein 4 (GCP4) caused enhanced bundling and disrupted dynamics of MTs, which resulted in longer stromules, but slower extension and retraction.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript using VIGS.

claim: Silencing GCP4 resulted in longer stromules, but slower extension and retraction.
source: Silencing the gene for γ-tubulin complex protein 4 (GCP4) caused enhanced bundling and disrupted dynamics of MTs, which resulted in longer stromules, but slower extension and retraction.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript using VIGS.

claim: Stromule extension does not require AFs.
source: Although stromule extension does not require AFs, they function as anchor points that stabilize stromules and anchor the body of chloroplasts.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing stromules extend in the presence of AF inhibitors.

claim: AFs function as anchor points that stabilize stromules and anchor the body of chloroplasts.
source: Although stromule extension does not require AFs, they function as anchor points that stabilize stromules and anchor the body of chloroplasts.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing stromules pause at AFs during retraction.

claim: AFs play an important role in type of chloroplast movement that appears to be directed by stromules.
source: AFs play an important role in type of chloroplast movement that appears to be directed by stromules.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing AF disruption affects stromule-directed chloroplast movement.

claim: Stromule-directed movement is completely disrupted by AF inhibitors.
source: This new type of stromule-directed movement is completely disrupted by AF inhibitors.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript using CTD treatment.

claim: Stromule-directed chloroplast movement was still observed when AFs were partially disrupted.
source: However, stromule-directed chloroplast movement was still observed when AFs were partially disrupted, suggesting that chloroplast anchoring might restrict stromule directed movement.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript using partial AF disruption.

claim: Chloroplast anchoring might restrict stromule directed movement.
source: However, stromule-directed chloroplast movement was still observed when AFs were partially disrupted, suggesting that chloroplast anchoring might restrict stromule directed movement.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that partial AF disruption still allows stromule-directed movement.

claim: A biological function of stromules is to direct the movement of chloroplasts.
source: We hypothesize that a biological function of stromules is to direct the movement of chloroplasts.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental observations presented in the manuscript.

claim: During an innate immune response, stromules extend along MTs towards nuclei and attach to the nuclei at actin anchor points.
source: During an innate immune response, we propose a model where stromules extend along MTs towards nuclei and attach to the nuclei at actin anchor points; and, these perinuclear stromule attachments guide chloroplasts to the nucleus.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental observations presented in the manuscript.

claim: Perinuclear stromule attachments guide chloroplasts to the nucleus during an immune response.
source: During an innate immune response, we propose a model where stromules extend along MTs towards nuclei and attach to the nuclei at actin anchor points; and, these perinuclear stromule attachments guide chloroplasts to the nucleus.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental observations presented in the manuscript.

claim: Stromules interact and extend along microtubules.
source: To examine the interactions of stromules with MTs, we expressed TagRFP fused to the N-terminal microtubule-associated protein domain of CKL6 (Ben-Nissan et al., 2008) (TagRFP-MAP-CKL6) in transgenic Nicotiana benthamiana plants expressing NRIP1 fused to Cerulean (NRIP1-Cerulean) that mark stromules (Caplan et al., 2015; Caplan et al., 2008). Marking both stromules and MTs revealed that these two structures overlapped in confocal microscopy images.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from confocal microscopy showing overlap between stromules and MTs.

claim: The varied morphology of stromules appeared to be correlated with MT interactions.
source: The varied morphology of stromules appeared to be correlated with MT interactions (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Stromules often initiate as beak-like structures.
source: Stromules often initiate as beak-like structures. The tips of beaks were seen interacting with MTs (Figure 1A; column 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The tips of beaks were seen interacting with MTs.
source: Stromules often initiate as beak-like structures. The tips of beaks were seen interacting with MTs (Figure 1A; column 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Beaks extend into longer stromules.
source: Beaks extend into longer stromules. Longer stromules were seen as just the tips of stromules interacting with MTs or the tip and the full length of the stromule aligned with MTs (Figure 1A; columns 2 and 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Longer stromules were seen as just the tips of stromules interacting with MTs or the tip and the full length of the stromule aligned with MTs.
source: Beaks extend into longer stromules. Longer stromules were seen as just the tips of stromules interacting with MTs or the tip and the full length of the stromule aligned with MTs (Figure 1A; columns 2 and 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: More complex stromule structures, such as kinked or branched stromules, were found at the junction of two MTs.
source: More complex stromule structures, such as kinked or branched stromules, were found at the junction of two MTs (Figure 1A; columns 4 and 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Approximately 11% of stromules did not interact with MTs.
source: However, approximately 11% of stromules did not interact with MTs (Figure 1A, arrowhead), suggesting there is a MT-independent mechanism of stromule formation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and quantification.

claim: There is a MT-independent mechanism of stromule formation.
source: However, approximately 11% of stromules did not interact with MTs (Figure 1A, arrowhead), suggesting there is a MT-independent mechanism of stromule formation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that some stromules do not interact with MTs.

claim: Microtubules were detected and described in plants using TEM and can readily be observed as hollow, tubule-like structures that are 24 nm in diameter.
source: Microtubules were originally detected and described in plants using TEM and can readily be observed as hollow, tubule-like structures that are 24 nm in diameter (Ledbetter and Porter, 1963).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: MTs were seen directly associated with the chloroplast outer envelope membrane at a kink point.
source: MTs were seen directly associated with the chloroplast outer envelope membrane at a kink point.
evidence: This claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Serial sections near the tip of a stromule that graze the chloroplast outer envelope membrane show MTs in line and in close proximity to the stromule.
source: Serial sections near the tip of a stromule that graze the chloroplast outer envelope membrane show MTs in line and in close proximity to the stromule.
evidence: This claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Stromules dynamically extended along MTs.
source: Time-lapse imaging of GFP-TUA6-labeled MTs revealed that stromules dynamically extended along MTs (Figure 1B, Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 1B and Video 1.

claim: Kymographs of the motion showed stromules extending and retracting in line with MTs in a single direction.
source: Kymographs of the motion showed stromules extending and retracting in line with MTs in a single direction (Figure 1B, left kymograph) or moving bi-directionally in opposite directions (Figure 1B, bottom right kymograph).
evidence: This claim is supported by kymograph analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Stromules move bi-directionally in opposite directions along MTs.
source: Kymographs of the motion showed stromules extending and retracting in line with MTs in a single direction (Figure 1B, left kymograph) or moving bi-directionally in opposite directions (Figure 1B, bottom right kymograph).
evidence: This claim is supported by kymograph analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Kymographs of the motion of stromules showed clear movement of stromule tips along MTs.
source: Kymographs of the motion of stromules showed clear movement of stromule tips along MTs (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by kymograph analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The velocity of stromule extension was significantly lower when MTs were marked with EB1-Citrine (0.0565 µm/s) compared to GFP-TUA6 (0.146 µm/s).
source: The velocity of stromule extension was significantly lower when MTs were marked with EB1-Citrine (0.0565 µm/s) compared to GFP-TUA6 (0.146 µm/s) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: All stromule extension was correlated with movement along MTs.
source: All stromule extension was correlated with movement along MTs.
evidence: This claim is supported by manual tracking of stromule velocities.

claim: Stromules and the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) have correlated dynamics and three-dimensional arrangement.
source: Stromules and the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) have correlated dynamics and three-dimensional arrangement; therefore, it was hypothesized that contact points along the ER direct their extension (Schattat et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: It was hypothesized that contact points along the ER direct stromule extension.
source: Stromules and the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) have correlated dynamics and three-dimensional arrangement; therefore, it was hypothesized that contact points along the ER direct their extension (Schattat et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Stromules were surrounded by ER.
source: Similar to the previous report (Schattat et al., 2011), stromules were surrounded by ER, but here we show that MTs direct the movement through ER (Figure 2A; Video 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Video 3.

claim: MTs direct the movement of stromules through ER.
source: Similar to the previous report (Schattat et al., 2011), stromules were surrounded by ER, but here we show that MTs direct the movement through ER (Figure 2A; Video 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Video 3.

claim: The ER forms channels around the stromules.
source: Imaging using a high-resolution airyscan confocal microscope revealed that the ER forms channels around the stromules, and MTs were found at the stromule-to-ER interface (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by high-resolution imaging data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: MTs were found at the stromule-to-ER interface.
source: Imaging using a high-resolution airyscan confocal microscope revealed that the ER forms channels around the stromules, and MTs were found at the stromule-to-ER interface (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by high-resolution imaging data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Stromule extension occurred actively along the MTs, while the ER changed its direction and formed a channel around the extended stromule tip.
source: Time lapse studies under similar imaging conditions showed that stromule extension occurred actively along the MTs, while the ER changed its direction and formed a channel around the extended stromule tip (Figure 2C, middle panel; Video 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 2C and Video 4.

claim: The stromule continued to extend along the MTs past the ER and no longer formed a channel around the extending stromule tip.
source: The stromule continued to extend along the MTs past the ER and no longer formed a channel around the extending stromule tip (Figure 2C, right panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Stromule extension is active along MTs and ER reorganization follows stromule extension along MTs.
source: These time-lapse studies indicate that stromule extension is active along MTs and ER reorganization follows stromule extension along MTs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the time-lapse imaging data.

claim: Depolymerization of MTs was noticeable 5 to 15 min after APM and Oryzalin treatment.
source: Compared to the DMSO vehicle control (Figure 3A, top panel), depolymerization of MTs was noticeable 5 to 15 min after APM and Oryzalin treatment, leaving behind remnants of partially depolymerized MTs and an increase of the MAP-CKL6 MT marker in the cytosol (Figure 3A, middle and bottom panels).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Mock control with DMSO resulted in an increase in stromules compared to the infiltration media control.
source: Although mock control with DMSO resulted in an increase in stromules compared to the infiltration media control, the APM or Oryzalin disruption of MTs for 15 min significantly inhibited this increase in stromule number (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: APM or Oryzalin disruption of MTs for 15 min significantly inhibited the increase in stromule number.
source: Although mock control with DMSO resulted in an increase in stromules compared to the infiltration media control, the APM or Oryzalin disruption of MTs for 15 min significantly inhibited this increase in stromule number (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: MT depolymerizers APM and Oryzalin not only decreased stromule number but also restricted stromules to MT fragments causing changes in stromule movement.
source: MT depolymerizers APM and Oryzalin not only decreased stromule number but also restricted stromules to MT fragments causing changes in stromule movement (Video 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Video 5.

claim: Beak-like protrusions from chloroplasts that did not result in stromules were observed in APM and Oryzalin treatment.
source: Beak-like protrusions from chloroplasts that did not result in stromules were also observed in APM and Oryzalin treatment (Figure 3A, asterisk; Video 5), however, we did not determine if these increased with the treatments compared to the DMSO vehicle control.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Video 5.

claim: Stromule length was gradually reduced during 15-min treatment with APM that was caused by stromule retraction and correlated with simultaneous depolymerization of the MTs.
source: In the time-lapsed data set shown in Figure 3A, stromule length was gradually reduced during 15-min treatment with APM that was caused by stromule retraction and correlated with simultaneous depolymerization of the MTs and, eventually, complete retraction of stromules (Figure 3A, middle and bottom panels, arrowhead).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The disappearance of stromules may be a combination of disruption of extended stromules and the prevention of induction of new stromules.
source: These results indicate that the disappearance of stromules may be a combination of disruption of extended stromules and the prevention of induction of new stromules.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: Infiltration of Paclitaxel-BODIPY conjugate into leaves showed extensive MT stabilization after 30 min of treatment compared to the mock control.
source: Infiltration of Paclitaxel-BODIPY conjugate into leaves of transgenic NRIP1-Cerulean N. benthamiana plants showed extensive MT stabilization after 30 min of treatment compared to the mock control (Figure 3C) and significantly induced stromules compared to mock control (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Paclitaxel treatment significantly induced stromules compared to mock control.
source: Infiltration of Paclitaxel-BODIPY conjugate into leaves of transgenic NRIP1-Cerulean N. benthamiana plants showed extensive MT stabilization after 30 min of treatment compared to the mock control (Figure 3C) and significantly induced stromules compared to mock control (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: After Paclitaxel treatment, long stromules and multiple stromules emanating from individual chloroplasts were observed.
source: Interestingly, after Paclitaxel treatment, we observed long stromules and multiple stromules emanating from individual chloroplasts (Figure 3C, bottom panels).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: MT stabilization is sufficient to induce stromules.
source: These results suggest that MT stabilization is sufficient to induce stromules.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Paclitaxel treatment results.

claim: GCP4 is a subunit of the γ-tubulin complex.
source: GCP4 is a subunit of the γ-tubulin complex and artificial miRNA (amiR)-mediated knockdown of Arabidopsis GCP4 resulted in hyper-parallel and bundled cortical MT in leaf epidermal cells (Kong et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Artificial miRNA (amiR)-mediated knockdown of Arabidopsis GCP4 resulted in hyper-parallel and bundled cortical MT in leaf epidermal cells.
source: GCP4 is a subunit of the γ-tubulin complex and artificial miRNA (amiR)-mediated knockdown of Arabidopsis GCP4 resulted in hyper-parallel and bundled cortical MT in leaf epidermal cells (Kong et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Four days after silencing, NbGCP4-silenced plants phenotypically looked similar to that of VIGS vector control plants.
source: Four days after silencing, NbGCP4-silenced plants phenotypically looked similar to that of VIGS vector control plants (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Six days post-silencing, leaves of the NbGCP4-silenced plants developed a crinkled leaf phenotype.
source: However, six days post-silencing, leaves of the NbGCP4-silenced plants developed a crinkled leaf phenotype (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, right panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: At six days post-silencing, the NRIP1-Cerulean stromule marker begin to leak out of chloroplasts compared to the VIGS control plants.
source: In addition, at this time point, the NRIP1-Cerulean stromule marker begin to leak out of chloroplasts compared to the VIGS control plants (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, right panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Fourteen days post-silencing, NbGCP4-silenced plants showed severe growth arrest and morphological distortion.
source: Fourteen days post-silencing, NbGCP4-silenced plants showed severe growth arrest and morphological distortion (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: At 4 days-post silencing, NbGCP4 mRNA levels are reduced by only 50% in the silenced plants compared to the VIGS control plants.
source: Although at 4 days-post silencing, NbGCP4 mRNA levels are reduced by only 50% in the silenced plants compared to the VIGS control plants (Figure 4B), cortical MT organization was significantly altered in the leaves of NbGCP4-silenced plants compared to the control (Figure 4A) in a similar way to amiR-AtGCP4 in Arabidopsis (Kong et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Cortical MT organization was significantly altered in the leaves of NbGCP4-silenced plants compared to the control in a similar way to amiR-AtGCP4 in Arabidopsis.
source: Although at 4 days-post silencing, NbGCP4 mRNA levels are reduced by only 50% in the silenced plants compared to the VIGS control plants (Figure 4B), cortical MT organization was significantly altered in the leaves of NbGCP4-silenced plants compared to the control (Figure 4A) in a similar way to amiR-AtGCP4 in Arabidopsis (Kong et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and citation to published literature.

claim: MTs were more parallel or aligned in NbGCP4-silenced plants compared to the vector control.
source: SOAX analysis showed that MTs were more parallel or aligned in NbGCP4-silenced plants compared to the vector control (Figure 4C), which was visible by displaying the MT direction by color-coding the azimuthal angles (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by SOAX analysis shown in Figure 4C-D.

claim: Silencing NbGCP4 decreases the curvature of MTs.
source: Quantitative SOAX analysis shows that silencing NbGCP4 decreases the curvature (Figure 4E) and increases the snake length fitted to MTs (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by SOAX analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Silencing NbGCP4 increases the snake length fitted to MTs.
source: Quantitative SOAX analysis shows that silencing NbGCP4 decreases the curvature (Figure 4E) and increases the snake length fitted to MTs (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by SOAX analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The alteration in MT organization at four days-post silencing of NbGCP4 resulted in more than twice the number of stromules in NbGCP4-silenced plants compared to the VIGS vector control.
source: The alteration in MT organization at four days-post silencing of NbGCP4 (Figure 4), resulted in more than twice the number of stromules in NbGCP4-silenced plants compared to the VIGS vector control (Figure 5A, top panels; 5B, compare bars in mock treatment).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: Stromules were on average significantly longer in NbGCP4-silenced plants compared to VIGS vector control.
source: Stromules were on average significantly longer in NbGCP4-silenced plants compared to VIGS vector control (Figure 5A, top panels; Figure 5C, compare bars in mock treatment).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5A and 5C.

claim: A greater percentage of stromules were longer than 3 μm in NbGCP4-silenced plants.
source: Furthermore, a greater percentage of stromules were longer than 3 μm in NbGCP4-silenced plants (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In NbGCP4-silenced plants, stromule movements were more constant than those in VIGS vector control.
source: We classified stromule movement into three types, smooth and constant movement, sudden and erratic movement, and side and tangential movement (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) and found that, in NbGCP4-silenced plants, stromule movements were more constant than those in VIGS vector control (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Stromules are significantly induced during N NLR-mediated immunity to TMV.
source: We recently reported that stromules are induced significantly during an immune response against bacterial and viral infections (Caplan et al., 2015). The nucleotide-binding domain leucine-rich repeat (NLR) immune receptor N recognizes p50 effector from Tobacco Mosaic Virus (TMV) and activate immune response to limit TMV to the infection site (Whitham et al., 1994). The stromules are significantly induced during N NLR-mediated immunity to TMV (Caplan et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The stromule angle and the angle of chloroplast movement are significantly correlated.
source: We compared 33 pairs for DMSO control and 47 pairs for ORY to calculate a circular correlation coefficient, r(FL) (Fisher and Lee, 1983). An r(FL) value of 1.0 would indicate that the stromule angle and the angle of chloroplast movement are always identical, an r(FL) of −1.0 would mean the paired angles differ by 180 degrees, and if the angles are randomly matched the r(FL) will be close to zero. The r(FL) values for DMSO and ORY were 0.76 and 0.85, respectively. To test the statistical significance, each data set was randomly shuffled 10,000 times and the r(FL) calculated for each randomization; the observed f(FL) values were greater than all the randomized r(FL) values, so for both DMSO and ORY the stromule angle and the angle of chloroplast movement were significantly correlated (p<0.0001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.
